turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. Well, I made this appointment because... I spend far too much of my day checking on things. I keep opening the same folders, my desk drawers, and these labeled boxes I have, just again and again. I have to make sure that my important papers and keepsakes are exactly where I left them. 

It's very frustrating, because I'll go back and do this even when I just checked them a few minutes before. It's just taking up too much of my time now, and I need it to stop.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient reports repetitively checking folders, desk drawers, and boxes to verify items are in place, even minutes after checking, which represents checking compulsions.

turns.doctor_question: When you resist the urge to check these folders and boxes, or if you can't check them, do you feel anxious or very uncomfortable?
turns.patient_response:
Well... it's just like I mentioned. If I try to hold off, I just end up going right back to open those same folders and labeled boxes anyway. I just have to make absolutely sure my papers and keepsakes are exactly where I left them. 

I don't really know how else to describe the feeling, other than I just have to do it, again and again. Even if I just checked them a few minutes before, the urge just pushes me right back to those drawers.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes repetitive checking compulsions, repeatedly opening the same folders, drawers, and boxes to ensure papers and keepsakes are in place despite having just checked moments earlier.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel that urge to check the folders and boxes, and you try to resist it, do you experience anxiety or a sense of dread that builds up until you give in and check them?
turns.patient_response:
I don't know if "dread" is the right word for it. I don't really feel frightened or panicked, if that's what you mean. It's more that... well, I just feel incredibly unsettled. 

If I try to sit down and read a book or watch a television program, my mind just won't let it go. The thought just sits there, nagging at me, until I finally get up and go look at the boxes again. So, I haven't really noticed it as anxiety, exactly... just a pressure that I can't ignore until I see with my own eyes that everything is still in its place.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient reports persistent, nagging thoughts that their mind won't let go of when attempting to do other activities.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes feeling an irresistible pressure to repeatedly check the boxes to verify that everything remains in its place.

turns.doctor_question: When you have the thought that you need to check those folders and boxes, do you recognize that this thought doesn't really make sense, or do you believe that something bad will actually happen if you don't check them?
turns.patient_response:
I do know it doesn't make sense. I mean, I know perfectly well that no one has been in the house to move my things. And... no, I don't really think anything bad is going to happen if I don't check. I'm not worried about a burglary or a fire or anything terrible like that. 

It's just... well, knowing it's silly doesn't seem to make the feeling go away. Even though I know the papers are exactly where I left them, I just have to see them with my own eyes to get that nagging thought out of my head.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient describes persistent, intrusive 'nagging thoughts' about their belongings that they recognize as irrational but cannot dismiss.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient reports an urge to engage in checking behaviors ('I just have to see them with my own eyes') to relieve the distress caused by the nagging thoughts.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing this urge to repeatedly check your folders and boxes? Has this been going on for weeks, months, or longer?
turns.patient_response: Well, let me think. I'm not entirely sure exactly when it started. It's been going on for a while now, but I couldn't give you a precise number of weeks or months. It just sort of became a habit over time, I suppose.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to about a year ago, were you already doing this checking behavior regularly, or did it start more recently than that?
turns.patient_response: I really couldn't say for sure. A year ago... well, I don't remember if I was doing it then or not. I'm sorry, I just haven't kept track of when it all started.

turns.doctor_question: On a typical day, roughly how much total time would you say you spend checking these folders and boxes? Is it minutes, an hour, several hours?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... it's definitely not just a few minutes. I'd say I spend far too much of my day doing it, which is really why I finally came in to see someone. It easily adds up to hours. 

I just keep opening the same folders, the drawers, and those labeled boxes again and again. I have to make sure my important papers and keepsakes are exactly where I left them. And... well, I'll do it even when I just checked them a few minutes before. So it really takes up a great deal of my time.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes spending hours each day repeatedly opening folders, drawers, and boxes to check that important papers and keepsakes are in place, confirming checking compulsions.

turns.doctor_question: When you're checking these folders and boxes repeatedly, do you think to yourself that this checking is excessive or unnecessary, or does it feel completely reasonable and justified to you at the time?
turns.patient_response: Well, I know it's excessive. I mean, I realize I just looked in that box five minutes ago, so I shouldn't need to look again. It doesn't really make sense to me why I have to do it, but... I just feel like I have to. So, yes, I know it's unnecessary, but I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it anyway.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient acknowledges engaging in repetitive, excessive checking behaviors (looking into boxes repeatedly) that feel unnecessary yet uncontrollable, confirming compulsions.

turns.doctor_question: Before you get the urge to check the boxes, do you ever have unwanted thoughts or images that pop into your head that bother you—like worries about something being wrong, or something bad happening—or does the urge to check just come to you without any particular thought triggering it?
turns.patient_response: Well, yes, it's usually a specific thought that starts it. Even when I know better, a thought will just... keep needling me. I'll start worrying that I might have accidentally thrown away my husband's old tax papers, or maybe that I put a family recipe in the wrong box. It just pops into my head, and I can't seem to let it pass without feeling like I've done something terribly careless. That's usually when I have to get up and go look.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient describes intrusive, persistent doubts and worries (such as accidentally discarding important papers or misplacing recipes) that repeatedly pop into their head and cause distress despite knowing better.

turns.doctor_question: When you have that thought about accidentally throwing away your husband's tax papers or putting a recipe in the wrong box, do you try to push the thought away or ignore it, or do you accept it and just check to make sure?
turns.patient_response: I do try to push it away. I really do. I tell myself, "You just looked, everything is fine." But... the thought just stays there. It keeps needling me. I try to ignore it and go back to reading or watching television, but I just can't seem to let it pass. The feeling that I've done something terribly careless just builds and builds until I give in and check.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient describes persistent, intrusive thoughts that keep needling her and that she unsuccessfully tries to ignore and push away, characteristic of obsessions.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient reports that distressing feelings build until she gives in and performs checking behavior in response to the intrusive thoughts.

turns.doctor_question: When you have these thoughts about throwing away the tax papers or putting the recipe in the wrong box, do you believe deep down that there's a real possibility you actually did those things, or do you know for certain that you didn't do them?
turns.patient_response: Well, I know I didn't do it. I mean, I know for certain I didn't throw those papers away or misplace the recipe. It's just... the thought is there, and even though I know it's not true, I just can't shake the feeling until I look. So, no, I don't really believe I did it. I just have to check anyway.
